 TO THE HONORABLE ADMIISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE:

    Charles Shell on behalf of 2833 Ranch, LP, CSR Ranches LP, and himself, pro se, files this

Initial Brief and respectfully shows as follows:


                                           I.    INTRODUCTION

    A robust electrical transmission system is necessary for today’s modern electrical grid. All

parties can agree that the system should be designed and operated in the safest practical manner.

Having reviewed Oncor/LCRA TSC application, testimony, and rebuttal testimony and listened

to their expert panel’s testimony at the Hearing on the Merits, it does not appear that the

applicants have given sufficient consideration in the route selection and design process to

reasonably mitigating risks associated with traversing along and/or across high-pressure natural

gas pipelines. Collocation and crossing pipelines increases the risks of pipeline failure and a

catastrophic explosion. These risks are especially amplified in areas where the insulators can

become contaminated by airborne pollution, like that generated by quarries. As such, certain

links that contain both quarries and pipelines, such as F43, should be avoided, and standard

ordering language should be adopted that strengthens risk mitigation. The public deserves the

safest possible route and system operation.

    E. Route

        8. Weighing the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC §
           25.101(b)(3)(B), which proposed transmission line route is the best alternative?

             After weighing the factors set forth in the applicable statute and rule, the best

        alternative route are routes: Route 894 (preferred by Oncor/LCRA) and then Route 487

        (recommended by PUC staff). However, these routes should be tweaked to ensure that

        high-pressure natural gas pipelines 42 inches in diameter or greater are crossed at 90

        degrees and only paralleled with a 2500 foot or more space between the pipeline and

        power line.

             Of the eight routes identified on the Intervenor Map Routes of Interest1, Route 894

        had the fewest habitable structures within 500 feet at 85 and Route 487 had the next

        lowest at 96.

            Routes using Link F43 should be avoided because of the various safety and reliability

        issues caused by the link traversing an area that includes both high-pressure natural gas

        pipelines and limestone quarries. Link F43 has a convergence of issues that raise serious

        safety and reliability concerns, including:

                (a) traversing an active limestone quarry area for 6.5 miles2 and thereby

                    vastly increasing the likelihood of dust and pollution accumulating on

                    insulators3, which is associated with elevated risk of electric flashover

                    to ground4,

                (b) paralleling a pipeline corridor that includes a 48-inch-diameter high-

                    pressure natural gas, a 42-inch-diameter high-pressure natural gas, and

                    a 42-inch-diameter oil pipeline5, which are already (two) or will be

                    (one more) in place before the proposed transmission line is built6,

                (c) crossing those same pipelines at about a 20-degree angle7, and

                (d) a first of its kind in Texas 765 kV transmission line with an amp rating

                    of 5,382 A8.

             It is well-documented that transmission lines can interfere with pipelines, generating

        safety hazards and compromising pipeline integrity9. “Collocated pipelines, sharing,

        paralleling, or crossing high voltage power line rights-of-way (ROW), may be subject to

        electrical interference from electrostatic coupling, electromagnetic inductive, and

        conductive effects. If the interference effects are high enough, they may pose a safety

        hazard to personnel or the public, or may compromise the integrity of the pipeline.”10

            In the event of a pipeline failure, the blast radius for the 48-inch Eiger Express

        pipeline would be an estimated 1257 feet11. The proposed F43 link parallels the Eiger

        Express pipeline for about 1200 feet12 with about 200 feet between the pipeline and the

        proposed link13. A pipeline failure would not only pose a huge safety risk to personnel

        and property within a ¼ mile of the failure, but also likely interrupt transmission line

        operation.

            Link F43 parallels and crosses these high-pressure natural gas pipelines and oil

        pipeline in an area with high quarry activity, increasing the likelihood of dust

        accumulation14 and associated flashovers15. Applicants stated that they would wash

        contaminated insulators after a flashover occurs16. This is concerning from a pipeline

        integrity perspective as “during a phase-to-ground fault on a power line, an adjacent or

         crossing pipeline may be subject to both resistive and inductive interference. Although

        these faults are normally of short duration (generally less than one second), pipeline

        damage can occur from high potential breakdown of the coating and conductive arching

        across the coating near the fault. Further, the fault current is typically carried by a single

        conductor, resulting in short term elevated induced voltages that can reach thousands of

        volts or greater. This presents significant risk to personnel in contact with the pipeline or

        electrically continuous appurtenance during a fault.”17

             Link F43 is routed in such a way that it increases the severity of various risk factors

        for high voltage interference with the high-pressure natural gas pipeline18:

                 (a) paralleling the pipelines at 200 foot offset rather than 2500 feet of offset,

                 (b) paralleling the pipeline (collocation) for about 1200 feet,

                 (c) crossing the pipeline at an angle of less than 30 degrees rather than greater

                     than 60 degrees.

             Applicants respond to safety concerns about the proposed transmission line’s

        proximity to natural gas pipelines by citing “compliance with industry practices and

        standards”, institutional knowledge, and past experience19. But the applicants’ failure to

        abide by published industry standards to mitigate risks around pipelines and the very

        nature of the project call this response into question. The Eiger Express pipeline at 48

        inches in diameter is one of the largest, if not the largest, high-pressure natural gas

        pipelines to be built and operated in the United States. The proposed 765kV transmission

         line will not only be the highest voltage line in the United States but will also be one of

        the first built in Texas and the first built by these TSPs. Putting two largest-of-their-kind

        infrastructure projects together, each carrying a tremendous amount of energy and one of

        a kind never operated in this state or by these TSPs, should be avoided. If this interaction

        cannot be avoided, the design process should require the strictest level of risk evaluation

        and safety constraints, rather than relying on inadequate or irrelevant past experience and

        generic reference to industry standards. Published recommendations on crossing and

        paralleling pipelines should be adhered to and specific risk analyses for the interaction of

        this particular transmission line with these specific pipelines should be completed. TSPs

        should not only be required to coordinate with the pipelines but to address and mitigate

        any risks identified in the risk analyses and design/route the transmission line to

        proactively avoid dangers.

            The simple fact that a utility has not experienced a safety event does not mean that

        their system has all the appropriate safety protocols built into it. The issue of electric

        blasting caps illustrates this point. Oncor/LCRA TSC stated that they are not familiar

        with distance limits associated with the use of electric blasting caps near power lines20.

        This contrasts with public information provided by several other utilities and has the

        potential to create a safety hazard for personnel working in limestone quarries within

        1000 feet21 of the proposed power lines.

      G. Best Management Practices

        14. Are the best management practices for construction and operating transmission
            facilities that are standard in the Commission's electric CCN orders adequate?
            If not, what additional practices should be required for the proposed
            transmission facilities?

                  Applicants made several comments, along with route design and the absence of

            certain information leaves the impression that Applicants need a little more focus on

            public safety. Some of the observations are:

            a.     Neither company appears to have publicly available information for landowners

                   regarding the safety issues related to high-voltage power lines like those of

                   other public utilities22.

            b.     Applicants’ witness was unfamiliar with safety issues related to the use of

                   electric blasting caps within 1000 feet of the electric lines23.

             c.    Applicants’ witness was unfamiliar with potential damage to high-pressure

                   natural gas pipelines resulting from a phase to ground insulator flashover24.

            d.     Applicant does not appear to use routing design to minimize safety issues

                   associated with crossing and/or paralleling high-pressure natural gas lines.



                  More awareness and attention to public safety is warranted. The following

            additional practices should be required in accordance with criteria provided by

             Interstate Natural Gas Association of America (INGAA) for pipelines co-existing

            with power lines25, 26:

             a.    Transmission facilities crossing natural gas pipelines that have diameters of 42

                   inches or larger shall be crossed at a 90 degree angle (perpendicular) to the

                   pipeline where possible but no less than a 60 degree angle to the pipeline.

            b.     Transmission facilities shall not parallel natural gas pipelines that have

                   diameters of 42 inches or larger any closer than 2500 feet.

             c.    Transmission facilities that cross natural gas pipelines that have diameters of 42

                   inches or larger and in close proximity of pollution sources like limestone

                   quarries shall utilize insulators with special coatings to prevent buildup of

                   pollutants which could cause insulator flashover and thus reliability and safety

                   issues.

            d.     Oncor / LCRA TSC should prepare and provide to all impacted landowners a

                   pamphlet outlining how to live and work safely around power lines similar to

                   the ones issued by other electric utilities27. This requirement should be included

                   in an ordering paragraph.

            b.     What benefit, if any, will the proposed practice provide?

                       These additional practices provide for improved public safety and system

                                          IV.      CONCLUSION

    Routes 894 or 487 should be selected. Routes using Link F43 should not be selected for

safety and reliability reasons. However, these routes should be tweaked to ensure that high-

pressure natural gas pipelines 42 inches in diameter or greater are crossed at 90 degrees and only

paralleled with a 2500 foot or more space between the pipeline and power line.

    More attention to safety issues are warranted. The proposed ordering paragraphs included in

Section V should be included in the order to improve public safety and system reliability.



                           V.     PROPOSED ORDERING PARAGRAPHS


Intervenor requests that the ALJs include the following additional ordering paragraphs:

1. Oncor/LCRA must conduct surveys, if not already completed, to identify metallic pipelines
   that could be affected by the transmission line approved by this Order and cooperate with
   metallic pipeline owners in modeling and analyzing potential hazards because of alternating-
   current interference affecting metallic pipelines being paralleled.


Initial Brief of Charles Shell, 2833 Ranch, LP, CSR Ranches, LP
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 17 of 18
 2. Oncor/LCRA must consult with pipeline owners or operators in the vicinity of the approved
   route regarding the pipeline owners' or operators' assessment of the need to install measures
   to mitigate the effects of alternating-current interference on existing metallic pipelines that
   are paralleled and / or crossed by the electric transmission facilities approved by this Order.

3. Oncor/LCRA must cooperate with pipeline or operators in vicinity of the approved route
   with a diameter of 42 inches or more to implement minor deviations in the approved route to
   mitigate the effects of alternating-current interference on existing metallic pipelines that are
   paralleled and / or crossed by the electric transmission facilities approved by this Order. Any
   minor deviations from the approved route must only directly affect landowners who were
   sent notice of the transmission line in accordance with 16 Texas Administrative Code section
   22.52(a)(3) and have agreed to the minor deviation.

4. Oncor/LCRA must utilize coated insulators in areas where landowners identify limestone
   quarry as a current or potential use of their property.

5. Oncor/LCRA must prepare and distribute to every affected landowner a Safety Pamphlet
   explaining the various landowner safety issues related to Living and Working around high
   voltage power lines including but not limited to flying kites, outdoor burning, pacemakers,
   climbing on towers, grounding of nearby structures, shooting, wire fences, underground
   pipes, irrigation systems, blasting, etc.

                                           I.    INTRODUCTION

    A robust electrical transmission system is necessary for today' s modern electrical grid. All

parties can agree that the system should be designed and operated in the safest practical manner.

Having reviewed Oncor/LCRA TSC application, testimony, and rebuttal testimony and listened

to their expert panel' s testimony at the Hearing on the Merits, it does not appear that the

applicants have given sufficient consideration in the route selection and design process to

reasonably mitigating risks associated with traversing along and/or across high-pressure natural

gas pipelines. Collocation and crossing pipelines increases the risks of pipeline failure and a

catastrophic explosion. These risks are especially amplified in areas where the insulators can

become contaminated by airborne pollution, like that generated by quarries. As such, certain

links that contain both quarries and pipelines, such as F43, should be avoided, and standard

ordering language should be adopted that strengthens risk mitigation. The public deserves the

safest possible route and system operation.

                                          IV.      CONCLUSION

    Routes 894 or 487 should be selected. Routes using Link F43 should not be selected for

safety and reliability reasons. However, these routes should be tweaked to ensure that high-

pressure natural gas pipelines 42 inches in diameter or greater are crossed at 90 degrees and only

paralleled with a 2500 foot or more space between the pipeline and power line.

    More attention to safety issues are warranted. The proposed ordering paragraphs included in

Section V should be included in the order to improve public safety and system reliability.



                           V.     PROPOSED ORDERING PARAGRAPHS


Intervenor requests that the ALJs include the following additional ordering paragraphs:

1. Oncor/LCRA must conduct surveys, if not already completed, to identify metallic pipelines
   that could be affected by the transmission line approved by this Order and cooperate with
   metallic pipeline owners in modeling and analyzing potential hazards because of alternating-
   current interference affecting metallic pipelines being paralleled.

 2. Oncor/LCRA must consult with pipeline owners or operators in the vicinity of the approved
   route regarding the pipeline owners' or operators' assessment of the need to install measures
   to mitigate the effects of alternating-current interference on existing metallic pipelines that
   are paralleled and/or crossed by the electric transmission facilities approved by this Order.

3. Oncor/LCRA must cooperate with pipeline or operators in vicinity of the approved route
   with a diameter of 42 inches or more to implement minor deviations in the approved route to
   mitigate the effects of alternating-current interference on existing metallic pipelines that are
   paralleled and / or crossed by the electric transmission facilities approved by this Order. Any
   minor deviations from the approved route must only directly affect landowners who were
   sent notice of the transmission line in accordance with 16 Texas Administrative Code section
   22.52(a)(3) and have agreed to the minor deviation.

4. Oncor/LCRA must utilize coated insulators in areas where landowners identify limestone
   quarry as a current or potential use of their property.

5. Oncor/LCRA must prepare and distribute to every affected landowner a Safety Pamphlet
   explaining the various landowner safety issues related to Living and Working around high
   voltage power lines including but not limited to flying kites, outdoor burning, pacemakers,
   climbing on towers, grounding of nearby structures, shooting, wire fences, underground
   pipes, irrigation systems, blasting, etc.
